tool.name: Jenkins
tool.tagline: Self-hosted automation server for CI/CD pipelines written as code
tool.description: Jenkins is an open-source automation server that builds, tests and deploys software through pipelines defined in a Jenkinsfile. You run it yourself, extend it with more than a thousand plugins and distribute work across agents. It remains one of the most widely deployed CI/CD systems, especially in enterprises with on-premise infrastructure and long-lived build setups.

glossary.def: The central Jenkins server: it shows the website you use Jenkins through, stores settings and build history, and decides which agent runs each build.
A machine (real, virtual or a container) connected to a Jenkins controller that actually runs builds.
A slot on a Jenkins agent that can run one build (or one parallel branch) at a time. Each agent has a set number of them.
In Jenkins, a short tag on an agent, such as linux or docker, that pipelines use to ask for a suitable machine.
In Jenkins, a configured task (also called an item or project) that can be run again and again. Each run is called a build.
In Jenkins, any machine that can run builds: an agent, or the controller's own built-in node.
A text file, usually at the top of a repository, containing a Jenkins pipeline written as code.
The folder where Jenkins keeps everything: jobs, build history, plugins, settings and stored credentials.
Long-term support: a release line that changes less often and only gets tested fixes between releases, meant for serious use.
A Jenkins pipeline written in a fixed structure of nested blocks (pipeline, agent, stages, steps, post), which Jenkins can check and display easily.
The older, free-form way to write a Jenkins pipeline: plain Groovy code using steps like node and stage, with no fixed structure.
A programming language that runs on Java. Jenkinsfiles and shared libraries are written in it.
Source control management: Jenkins's term for version control systems such as Git.
In Jenkins, the folder on an agent where a build checks out the code and does its work. It is kept between builds unless you clean it.
Jenkins's encrypted storage for passwords, tokens, keys and secret files, each saved under an ID that pipelines refer to.
A Jenkins build result meaning the build itself ran, but something, usually failing tests, needs attention.
A Jenkins job that points at a repository and automatically creates a child job for every branch and pull request that has a Jenkinsfile.
A Jenkins folder that scans a whole GitHub organisation or GitLab group and creates a Multibranch Pipeline for every repository with a Jenkinsfile.
The Jenkins plugin that connects a Multibranch Pipeline to a hosting site such as GitHub or GitLab, finding branches and pull requests and reporting results back.
In Jenkins, a pipeline directive that creates one parallel stage for every combination of axis values, such as each operating system with each Java version.
In Jenkins, saving some files from one stage's workspace (through the controller) so a later stage, possibly on another agent, can unstash them.
In Jenkins, a Git repository of reusable pipeline code (custom steps and classes) that Jenkinsfiles load with @Library.
Jenkins's safety check for pipeline code: only method calls on an allowed list, or approved by an administrator, may run.
Continuation-passing style: how Jenkins rewrites pipeline Groovy so its state can be saved after every step and the build can resume after a restart.
The @NonCPS annotation: marks a Groovy method to run as normal, faster code, without CPS. Such a method can't call pipeline steps.
Jenkins Configuration as Code: a plugin that sets up the whole controller (security, credentials, agents, libraries) from YAML files.
A Jenkins agent created fresh for one build, such as a new container or virtual machine, and deleted afterwards.

concepts.name: Controller, agents, jobs and plugins
concepts.summary: How Jenkins is organised: a controller that hands out work, agents that run it, and plugins that add almost every feature.
concepts.why: Knowing which part does what explains Jenkins's settings screens, how it grows, and most of the ways it breaks.
concepts.body:
Every time someone pushes a commit, a team wants the same checks: does the code still build, do the tests still pass? And when all is well, the new version should be shipped. Doing that by hand is slow and gets forgotten. **CI/CD** automates it: continuous integration (CI) checks every change, and continuous delivery or deployment (CD) ships it. **Jenkins** is a program that does this. It's written in Java, and unlike hosted services you install and run it on your own machines.

Its main parts:

- The **controller** is the central server. It shows the website you use Jenkins through, stores settings and build history in a folder called `JENKINS_HOME`, and decides which machine runs each piece of work.
- **Agents** are the machines that do the work: virtual machines, containers, or servers. Each agent has a number of **executors**: slots, each able to run one build at a time. Agents carry **labels** such as `linux` or `docker`, so work can ask for a suitable machine.
- **Jobs** (also called items or projects) say what to build. The modern kind is a **Pipeline** job: its steps are written in a text file called a **Jenkinsfile**, kept with the code. Older Freestyle jobs are set up by filling in settings pages on the website, which makes changes to them hard to track.
- A **build** is one run of a job, numbered #1, #2, ... Each has a log of its output, a result, and any files it kept.
- **Plugins** are add-ons, and they provide nearly everything: Git support, Pipeline itself, stored passwords, Docker agents, notifications. A typical installation has dozens.

A build usually starts from a trigger: a message from GitHub or GitLab when someone pushes (a **webhook**: an automatic web request one service sends another when something happens), a schedule, a check of the repository for changes every few minutes, another job finishing, or a person clicking **Build Now**.

Compared with hosted CI services, Jenkins gives you full control over hardware, network and plugins, at the cost of running, upgrading and securing the server yourself.
takeaways: The controller hands out work and stores everything; agents run builds on their executors
Pipeline jobs are written as code in a Jenkinsfile
Plugins supply most features, including Git and Pipeline
pitfalls: Running builds on the controller itself; it should only coordinate.

quiz.q: What is an executor in Jenkins?
options: A plugin that runs shell commands
A slot on an agent that can run one build at a time
quiz.explain: Each agent has a set number of executors; each one runs one build (or one parallel branch of a build) at a time.

concepts.name: Installing Jenkins with Docker
concepts.summary: Start a Jenkins LTS controller in Docker with a volume that keeps its data, unlock it and install the suggested plugins.
concepts.why: A Jenkins of your own, which you can rebuild in a minute, is the fastest way to learn pipelines and to test changes before touching a shared server.
concepts.body:
Jenkins comes as a Java program file (a WAR file), as packages for Linux distributions, and as the official Docker image `jenkins/jenkins`. For anything serious, use the **LTS** line: long-term support releases come out every 12 weeks and only receive tested fixes in between, while weekly releases get new features first. Current Jenkins LTS needs **Java 21 or 25** (support for Java 17 ended with version 2.555.1). The image tag `lts-jdk21` includes Java 21.

Everything Jenkins knows lives in `JENKINS_HOME` (`/var/jenkins_home` inside the image): jobs, build history, plugins, stored passwords and keys. Containers lose their files when they are replaced, so keep this folder in a **Docker volume**: a storage area Docker manages outside any container, attached to a folder inside one. That way the data survives upgrades. Back it up too.

On first start Jenkins writes a one-time administrator password to `secrets/initialAdminPassword` and prints it in its log. Open `http://localhost:8080`, paste it, choose **Install suggested plugins** (Git, Pipeline, credentials and more), then create an administrator user.

Ports: `8080` for the website, `50000` for agents that connect to the controller themselves (agents that connect over an ordinary web connection can use 8080 instead).

Upgrading mostly means changing the image tag and restarting, then updating plugins under **Manage Jenkins, Plugins**. Read the LTS upgrade guide first; plugins that don't yet work with the new version are the usual source of trouble.
concepts.code:
docker volume create jenkins_home
docker run -d --name jenkins --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8080:8080 -p 50000:50000 \
  -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home \
  jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21

# the one-time password for the setup screen
docker exec jenkins cat /var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword
# 3f2a9c... (32 characters)

docker logs -f jenkins     # ... Jenkins is fully up and running
takeaways: Use the LTS line; Jenkins needs Java 21 or 25
JENKINS_HOME holds everything: keep it in a volume and back it up
Unlock with initialAdminPassword, then install the suggested plugins
pitfalls: Running the container without a volume and losing every job on the next upgrade.

options: All jobs, history, plugins and stored passwords live there and must survive replacing the container
Jenkins refuses to start without it
quiz.explain: JENKINS_HOME is Jenkins's entire state; without a volume it disappears with the container.

concepts.name: Your first declarative pipeline
concepts.summary: Write a declarative pipeline with agent, stages and steps, and read its stage view and console output.
concepts.why: Declarative pipeline syntax is how almost all new Jenkins jobs are written.
concepts.body:
A **pipeline** is the series of steps a build goes through, such as build, then test, then deploy. In Jenkins you write it as code in **Groovy**, a programming language that runs on Java. You don't need to know Groovy: a **declarative pipeline** uses a fixed structure of nested blocks, and most lines are just commands to run. (Declarative means you describe what you want, not how to do it step by step.) The skeleton is always:

- `pipeline { }`: the outer block.
- `agent`: where to run. `agent any` means any free executor; later you'll pick machines by label, or run inside containers.
- `stages { stage('Name') { steps { ... } } }`: named phases, shown as columns on the build's page.
- `steps`: the actual work, made of **steps** such as `sh` (run a shell command on Linux or macOS), `bat` or `powershell` (Windows), `echo` (print a message), `git`, `archiveArtifacts` and `junit`.

`sh` fails the stage and the build if the command's exit code isn't 0, and the later stages are skipped. A shell script of several lines goes between triple quotes: `'''...'''`.

Quoting matters, because this is Groovy. In a double-quoted string, Groovy replaces `${...}` with a Groovy value **before** the shell sees the text. In a single-quoted string, the text reaches the shell untouched, so the shell does the replacing. Use single quotes unless you really need a Groovy value.

To try it, create a job of type **Pipeline**, choose **Pipeline script** and paste the code. The **Snippet Generator** (the **Pipeline Syntax** link on the job's page) writes correct code for any installed step, and **Replay** lets you edit and rerun a build's script without committing: ideal while learning.
takeaways: pipeline > agent + stages > stage > steps
sh fails the build on a non-zero exit code
Single quotes: the shell replaces $VAR; double quotes: Groovy replaces ${...} first
pitfalls: Using double quotes around shell commands containing $, and getting Groovy errors or wrong values.

quiz.explain: In a double-quoted Groovy string, ${...} is replaced by Groovy first; here that fails or uses a Groovy variable instead.

concepts.name: Jenkinsfile in source control and webhooks
concepts.summary: Keep the pipeline as a Jenkinsfile in the repository, use Pipeline script from SCM, and start builds with webhooks instead of repeated checks.
concepts.why: With the pipeline stored as code, the build definition is versioned, reviewed and branched together with the application.
concepts.body:
Pasting scripts into a job's settings doesn't scale. Instead, commit a file named `Jenkinsfile` at the top of the repository, and set the job's definition to **Pipeline script from SCM**. **SCM** (source control management) is Jenkins's term for version control systems such as Git. You give it the repository's address, login details, the branch and the file's path.

At build time Jenkins fetches the Jenkinsfile from that branch. A declarative pipeline then automatically checks out the same commit into the **workspace**, the folder on the agent where the build does its work (you'll see this as a stage named **Declarative: Checkout SCM**). So `sh 'make'` sees your code. In custom code, `checkout scm` does the same explicitly.

How builds start:

- **Webhooks**: GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket send Jenkins a web request on every push, with the matching plugin installed (for example at `https://jenkins.example.com/github-webhook/`). Instant and cheap.
- **Polling** (checking again and again): `pollSCM('H/5 * * * *')` asks the repository for changes every five minutes. Use it only when the Git server can't reach Jenkins.

Environment variables describe the build: `BUILD_NUMBER`, `BUILD_URL`, `WORKSPACE`, `JOB_NAME`, and, with Git, `GIT_COMMIT` and `GIT_BRANCH`. Read them as `env.NAME` in Groovy, or as `$NAME` inside `sh`.

Changing the build now means making a commit: reviewed by teammates before merging, tested on a branch, and undoable like any other code.
takeaways: Commit a Jenkinsfile and use Pipeline script from SCM
Declarative pipelines check out the same commit automatically
Prefer webhooks to polling
pitfalls: Polling every minute from hundreds of jobs, overloading both Jenkins and the Git server.

quiz.q: With Pipeline script from SCM, which version of the Jenkinsfile is used for a build?
options: The one stored in the job's settings in Jenkins
The one in the configured branch of the repository
Always the one on the default branch
The newest file across all branches
quiz.explain: Jenkins reads the Jenkinsfile from the branch it builds, so the pipeline is versioned with the code.

concepts.name: post conditions, test reports and artifacts
concepts.summary: Run steps after a stage or the whole build with post, publish test results, and keep build outputs as artifacts.
concepts.why: Clean-up, notifications and test reports must happen even when the build fails, and that is exactly what post is for.
concepts.body:
A `post` section runs after the whole pipeline, or after a single stage, with blocks chosen by the result:

- `always`: whatever happened.
- `success`, `failure`, `unstable`, `aborted`: only on that result.
- `changed`, `fixed`, `regression`: compared with the previous build, useful for sending a message only when something changed.
- `cleanup`: last of all, after the other post blocks.

A build's result is **SUCCESS**, **UNSTABLE** (the build ran, but something needs attention, typically failing tests), **FAILURE**, or **ABORTED** (stopped early).

Two steps belong in almost every pipeline's `post`:

- `junit 'reports/*.xml'` reads test reports in the JUnit format (a widely used file layout for test results that most test tools can write), shows the failing tests and trends on the build's page, and marks the build UNSTABLE when tests fail.
- `archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'dist/**', fingerprint: true` keeps the listed files with the build, as **artifacts**, so people and other jobs can download them. The fingerprint lets Jenkins trace where a file was used.

The workspace stays on the agent between builds, so files left over from an earlier run can sneak into the next. `cleanWs()` (from the Workspace Cleanup plugin) or `deleteDir()` in `post { cleanup { } }` wipes it.

Also set a build discarder (covered with options, at the Practical level), so kept artifacts and logs don't fill the controller's disk.
takeaways: post blocks: always, success, failure, unstable, changed, fixed, cleanup
junit publishes test results and marks failures UNSTABLE
archiveArtifacts keeps build outputs with the build
pitfalls: Putting junit inside steps, after the test command: if the tests fail, that step never runs. Use post { always }.

quiz.q: Tests fail and junit records them, but every build command exits with 0. What is the build result?
quiz.explain: The junit step marks a build UNSTABLE when it finds failing tests.

concepts.name: Environment variables and credentials
concepts.summary: Define environment variables, keep secrets in the credentials store, and use them safely with credentials() and withCredentials.
concepts.why: Deploying and publishing need secrets, and Jenkins pipelines leak them easily if you bind or quote them wrong.
concepts.body:
`environment { }` at the pipeline or stage level sets environment variables for the steps inside it. Values can be plain strings or helper calls.

Secrets (passwords, tokens, keys) live in the **credentials store** (**Manage Jenkins, Credentials**, or a folder's own credentials), each saved under an ID. Types include secret text, username with password, SSH private key, and secret file. Two ways to use them:

- In `environment`: `TOKEN = credentials('api-token')`. For username-with-password credentials Jenkins also defines `NAME_USR` and `NAME_PSW`. For a secret file, the variable holds the path of a temporary copy.
- The `withCredentials([...]) { }` step makes them available only inside its block, with bindings such as `string`, `usernamePassword`, `file` and `sshUserPrivateKey`.

Jenkins hides bound secret values in the build log. The crucial rule: refer to secrets in **single-quoted** `sh` strings, so the shell does the replacing: `sh 'curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ...'`. With double quotes, Groovy pastes the secret into the command text itself, where it can show up in the list of running processes and in logs. Jenkins warns about this as "insecure interpolation".

Keep credentials narrowly scoped: store them in the folder of the jobs that need them rather than globally, so other teams' pipelines can't read them.
takeaways: environment {} sets variables; credentials('id') pulls in a stored secret
Username-with-password credentials add _USR and _PSW
Always refer to secrets inside single-quoted sh strings
pitfalls: sh "curl -u $USER:$PASS ..." with double quotes makes Groovy paste the secrets into the command text, exposing them.

quiz.q: Why prefer sh 'deploy --token $TOKEN' over sh "deploy --token $TOKEN" for a secret?
options: Hiding in logs only works with double quotes
Double quotes don't work in sh
With single quotes the shell replaces it, so the secret never lands in the Groovy string
quiz.explain: Groovy would paste the secret into the command text; shell replacement keeps it in the environment only.

concepts.name: Agents, labels and Docker containers
concepts.summary: Choose where stages run with agent labels, run steps inside Docker images, and use agent none for per-stage agents.
concepts.why: Builds need the right operating system, tools and isolation, and the agent directive is how you get them.
concepts.body:
The `agent` directive appears at the top of the pipeline or on a stage:

- `agent any`: any free executor.
- `agent { label 'linux && docker' }`: a **node** (any machine that runs builds) whose labels match the expression; `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not) are allowed.
- `agent { docker { image 'node:22' } }`: run the steps inside a container from that image, on a node that has Docker (Docker Pipeline plugin). Jenkins mounts the workspace into the container, so files persist across steps. `args` adds extra `docker run` options; `reuseNode true` keeps using the surrounding node's workspace.
- `agent { dockerfile true }`: first build the image from the repository's own Dockerfile.
- `agent { kubernetes { yaml ... } }`: a fresh pod (a Kubernetes unit of one or more containers) per build, thrown away afterwards (Kubernetes plugin).
- `agent none`: no pipeline-wide agent; each stage declares its own. Use it when stages need different platforms, or when a stage waits for a person's approval and shouldn't hold an executor meanwhile.

Containers give every build a clean, versioned set of tools without installing anything on the agents: an agent only needs Docker. Pin image tags, so a new `latest` doesn't break builds.

Agents connect to the controller in one of two ways: the controller logs in to them over SSH and starts them, or the agent connects to the controller itself (TCP port 50000, or a WebSocket). Cloud plugins create agents on demand and remove them when idle.
takeaways: agent { label '...' } picks nodes by a label expression
agent { docker { image ... } } runs steps in a pinned container
agent none plus per-stage agents mixes platforms and frees executors
pitfalls: Installing every tool on every agent instead of using pinned container images.

quiz.q: A pipeline has agent none at the top. What must each stage that runs steps have?
quiz.explain: With agent none there's no default; every stage that runs steps must declare an agent.

concepts.name: Options, parameters, triggers and when
concepts.summary: Add timeouts and build retention with options, ask for input with parameters, schedule builds, and run stages only when a condition holds.
concepts.why: These directives turn a basic pipeline into one that is safe to run unattended and adjustable per build.
concepts.body:
**options** configure the whole pipeline (some also work per stage):

- `timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES')`: stop builds that hang.
- `buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '30'))`: keep only the last 30 builds and their artifacts.
- `disableConcurrentBuilds()`: if a build is already running, queue the next one instead of running both at once.
- `retry(2)`, `skipDefaultCheckout()`, `timestamps()` (Timestamper plugin: a time next to every log line).

**parameters** define inputs shown on **Build with Parameters**: `string`, `booleanParam`, `choice`, `text`, `password`. Read them as `params.NAME`. Note that the first build after adding parameters runs before Jenkins knows about them.

**triggers** start builds automatically: `cron('H 2 * * 1-5')`, a schedule in the classic Unix **cron** format (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week: here hour 2 on weekdays), or `pollSCM(...)`, or another job finishing. The `H` symbol stands for a minute computed from the job's name, so it stays the same for that job but differs between jobs, spreading them out instead of all starting at minute 0.

**when** decides whether a stage runs: `branch 'main'`, `tag 'v*'`, `changeRequest()` (building a pull request), `environment name: 'DEPLOY', value: 'true'`, `expression { params.RUN_E2E }` (any Groovy condition), combined with `allOf`, `anyOf` and `not`. Add `beforeAgent true` so the condition is checked before an agent is taken.

The `input` step pauses the build for a human decision, such as approving a production deploy. Run it outside any agent, so it doesn't hold an executor while waiting.
takeaways: options: timeout, buildDiscarder and disableConcurrentBuilds belong in most pipelines
params.NAME reads build parameters
when { } skips stages; H spreads cron schedules
pitfalls: Writing cron('0 * * * *') on many jobs so they all start at the same minute; use H.

quiz.q: What does H mean in cron('H 2 * * *')?
options: A minute computed from the job's name, the same every time for that job
quiz.explain: H picks a fixed, pseudo-random minute per job, spreading the load across jobs.

concepts.name: Multibranch pipelines and pull requests
concepts.summary: Let Jenkins find every branch and pull request that has a Jenkinsfile, and build each one automatically.
concepts.why: Teams work on many branches at once; multibranch jobs give each one CI without setting up jobs by hand.
concepts.body:
A **Multibranch Pipeline** job points at a whole repository instead of one branch. Jenkins scans it, creates a child job for every branch that contains a `Jenkinsfile`, and deletes child jobs when their branches disappear. With a **branch source** plugin, such as GitHub Branch Source, it does the same for every pull request. An **Organization Folder** goes one level higher: it scans a whole GitHub organisation or GitLab group and sets up a Multibranch Pipeline for each repository.

Each child job builds its own branch's Jenkinsfile. Useful variables:

- `BRANCH_NAME`: the branch name, or `PR-42` for pull request number 42.
- `CHANGE_ID`, `CHANGE_TARGET`, `CHANGE_AUTHOR`: set only for pull requests.

`when { branch 'main' }` and `when { changeRequest() }` let one Jenkinsfile behave differently on main, on feature branches and on pull requests: test everywhere, deploy only from main.

With the GitHub or GitLab branch source plugins, webhooks start scans and builds immediately, and the result is reported back to the commit and shown on the pull request as a check.

Pull requests from forks (copies of the repository owned by outsiders) are a security concern: a fork could change the Jenkinsfile to print your secrets. Branch sources therefore have trust settings. By default, for a pull request from an untrusted fork, Jenkins takes the Jenkinsfile from the target branch, not from the pull request.
takeaways: Multibranch jobs create one child job per branch or pull request with a Jenkinsfile
BRANCH_NAME and CHANGE_* describe the branch or pull request
Pull requests from forks are untrusted: their Jenkinsfile changes aren't used by default
pitfalls: Creating one pipeline job per branch by hand.

quiz.q: In a multibranch job, what is env.BRANCH_NAME while building pull request #42?
quiz.explain: Pull request child jobs are named PR-<number>, and BRANCH_NAME follows that name.

concepts.name: Parallel stages and matrix
concepts.summary: Run independent stages at the same time with parallel, and cover combinations of operating systems and versions with matrix.
concepts.why: Running things at the same time is the main way to cut pipeline duration on a busy Jenkins.
concepts.body:
Inside a stage, `parallel { }` holds child stages that run at the same time, each possibly on its own agent. The build's graph view shows them side by side. `failFast true` (or `options { parallelsAlwaysFailFast() }`) stops the other branches as soon as one fails.

The **matrix** directive generates parallel stages from axes:

- `axes { axis { name 'OS'; values 'linux', 'windows' } axis { name 'JDK'; values '17', '21' } }` gives four cells, one per combination.
- `excludes { }` removes combinations.
- Inside each cell the axis values are environment variables, usable in `agent { label "${OS}" }` and in steps.

Each parallel branch takes up an executor while it runs, so parallelism is limited by what the agents offer: ten branches on a node with two executors mostly wait in the queue.

Branches share no files unless they happen to use the same workspace: two branches on the same node with `reuseNode`, or in the same folder, can overwrite each other's files. To pass files between stages, **stash** them: `stash` saves chosen files from the workspace and `unstash` restores them later, possibly on another agent. The files travel through the controller, so this is fine for small files only; use artifacts or outside storage for big ones.
takeaways: parallel { } runs child stages at the same time; failFast stops the others on a failure
matrix expands axes into parallel cells, with excludes
Parallelism is capped by the available executors
pitfalls: Using stash for large build outputs; the files pass through the controller.

quiz.q: A matrix has axes with 3 and 2 values and one exclude. How many cells run?
quiz.explain: 3 x 2 = 6 combinations, minus the one excluded.

concepts.name: Shared libraries
concepts.summary: Move common pipeline logic into a versioned Groovy library with vars/ steps and src/ classes, loaded with @Library.
concepts.why: With many repositories, a shared library keeps each Jenkinsfile short and lets one team fix the build logic everywhere at once.
concepts.body:
A **shared library** is a Git repository with a fixed layout:

- `vars/`: each file `name.groovy` defines a new pipeline step called `name`, implemented by the file's `call(...)` method. This is the part most teams use.
- `src/`: Groovy classes, organised in packages (folders), imported like any Groovy code.
- `resources/`: non-Groovy files, loaded with `libraryResource`.

Register the library under **Manage Jenkins, System, Global Trusted Pipeline Libraries** (or on a folder) with a name and a default version. A Jenkinsfile loads it with `@Library('ci-lib@v2.1') _`. The line is a Groovy annotation, and the trailing underscore is just something for it to attach to. If the library is set to load implicitly, no such line is needed.

A `vars` step can wrap a whole declarative pipeline, so an application's Jenkinsfile shrinks to one line: `standardJavaPipeline(deploy: true)`. Taking a `Map` (a set of named options) keeps that call readable and easy to extend.

In production, pin versions with Git tags; test a library change by pointing one job at a branch. Libraries registered globally are **trusted**: they run outside the Groovy sandbox (Jenkins's safety check on pipeline code) and can call any part of Jenkins, so changes to them deserve the same review as changes to Jenkins itself. Libraries registered on a folder run inside the sandbox.
takeaways: vars/name.groovy with call() becomes a pipeline step called name
Load with @Library('lib@version') _ and pin versions
Global libraries are trusted and skip the sandbox; review them carefully
pitfalls: Loading a library from a moving branch in production; one bad commit breaks every pipeline.

quiz.q: A file vars/notify.groovy defines def call(String msg). How is it used in a Jenkinsfile?
quiz.explain: Each file in vars/ becomes a pipeline step named after the file.

concepts.name: Scripted pipelines and the script block
concepts.summary: Know when declarative syntax isn't enough, use script { } for logic, and read scripted node/stage pipelines.
concepts.why: Many existing Jenkinsfiles are scripted, and real pipelines eventually need loops or stages made on the fly.
takeaways: Scripted pipelines use node/stage/try-catch instead of declarative blocks
script { } embeds Groovy logic in a declarative pipeline
Pipeline Groovy runs in a sandbox, with approvals, and is rewritten for restart safety
pitfalls: Using the loop variable itself inside the closures, so every branch sees the last value; copy it per loop round.

quiz.q: A pipeline fails with RejectedAccessException. What does it mean?
options: The Groovy sandbox blocked a method call that an admin hasn't approved
quiz.explain: Sandboxed pipeline code can only call methods on the allowed list or approved by an administrator.

concepts.name: CPS, durability and pipeline performance
concepts.summary: Why pipeline Groovy is rewritten into continuation-passing style, what survives a restart, and how to keep pipelines fast.
concepts.why: Odd serialization errors, slow pipelines and overloaded controllers all trace back to how pipelines execute.
concepts.body:
Pipeline Groovy runs on the **controller**, not on the agent; only steps like `sh` run on agents. To survive a controller restart, the Groovy is rewritten into **continuation-passing style** (CPS): after each step, the program's state (its variables and where it was) is written to disk, and a resumed build continues from there. Writing an object out and reading it back later is called **serialization**.

Consequences:

- A variable held across steps must be serializable (in Java terms, its class implements `Serializable`). Some objects aren't, such as a regular-expression `Matcher` or an iterator, and they cause `NotSerializableException`.
- A method annotated **@NonCPS** runs as normal Groovy, faster and without serialization, but it **cannot call pipeline steps** and isn't resumable.
- Heavy Groovy logic (reading through large files, big loops) uses the controller's CPU and slows down every other build. Do such work in `sh`, with a real program on the agent.

Durability settings trade safety for speed: `MAX_SURVIVABILITY` writes state often; `PERFORMANCE_OPTIMIZED` writes far less, so a crash may lose a running build's progress, but disk traffic drops drastically. Set it globally or with `options { durabilityHint('PERFORMANCE_OPTIMIZED') }`.

Scaling rules from the Jenkins docs: keep pipelines thin, use few steps (one `sh` running a script beats 200 tiny `sh` calls), avoid large stashes and huge logs, and give the controller zero executors.
takeaways: Pipeline Groovy runs on the controller, rewritten as CPS code with its state saved to disk
@NonCPS methods are plain Groovy and cannot call steps
PERFORMANCE_OPTIMIZED durability trades restart safety for much less disk traffic
pitfalls: Doing heavy parsing in pipeline Groovy, loading the controller instead of an agent.

options: Call pipeline steps such as sh or echo
quiz.explain: Steps require the CPS machinery; @NonCPS code runs as plain Groovy.

concepts.name: Configuration as Code and plugin management
concepts.summary: Define the whole Jenkins controller in YAML with JCasC, pin plugins in a file, and build a controller image you can rebuild any time.
concepts.why: A controller set up by hand drifts and can't be rebuilt after a disaster; one defined in code can.
concepts.body:
The Configuration as Code plugin (**JCasC**) reads YAML files describing the controller: system settings, how users log in, who may do what, credentials, cloud agents, global libraries and tool installations. Point it at the files with the `CASC_JENKINS_CONFIG` environment variable (a file, a folder or a URL). On startup, or when you click **Reload existing configuration**, Jenkins applies them. **Manage Jenkins, Configuration as Code, View Configuration** exports the current setup as a starting point.

Secrets in JCasC YAML are written as `${VAR}` and filled in from environment variables, from files (such as Kubernetes or Docker secrets) or from a secrets manager, never written out in the YAML itself.

Plugins are the other half of the state. List them with pinned versions in `plugins.txt` and install them while building the image, with `jenkins-plugin-cli`. Together this gives an **immutable** controller, one that is never changed in place: a Docker image containing Jenkins, the plugins and the JCasC files, plus a volume only for build history. An upgrade becomes a reviewed change to the image, which you can test and undo.

Jobs come from code too: Multibranch Pipelines and Organization Folders find Jenkinsfiles, and the Job DSL plugin can create other jobs from scripts. The goal is that nothing important exists only in the website's settings.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile for a controller image
FROM jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-Djenkins.install.runSetupWizard=false" \
    CASC_JENKINS_CONFIG=/casc
COPY plugins.txt /usr/share/jenkins/ref/plugins.txt
RUN jenkins-plugin-cli --plugin-file /usr/share/jenkins/ref/plugins.txt
COPY casc/ /casc/

# plugins.txt                     # casc/jenkins.yaml
# configuration-as-code:latest    # jenkins:
# workflow-aggregator:latest      #   numExecutors: 0
# git:latest                      #   securityRealm:
# (pin exact versions in prod)    #     local:
#                                 #       users:
#                                 #         - id: admin
#                                 #           password: ${ADMIN_PASSWORD}
takeaways: JCasC applies YAML from CASC_JENKINS_CONFIG at startup or on reload
Pin plugins in plugins.txt and install them with jenkins-plugin-cli
Secrets are ${VAR} references, filled in when the YAML is loaded
pitfalls: Changing settings on the website of a JCasC-managed controller; the next reload overwrites them.

quiz.q: What happens to a setting changed by hand on the website when the JCasC configuration is reloaded?
options: It is overwritten by the YAML value if the YAML defines it
It is merged into the YAML file
quiz.explain: JCasC treats the YAML as the single source of truth and applies it again.

concepts.name: Securing and scaling a Jenkins controller
concepts.summary: Run no builds on the controller, lock down who may do what and who can read credentials, and grow with agents created per build.
concepts.why: A Jenkins controller holds the keys to production; it's a top target for attackers and a frequent bottleneck.
concepts.body:
**Builds never run on the controller.** Set the built-in node's executors to 0. A build running on the controller can read `JENKINS_HOME`, including the stored credentials and the key that decrypts them.

**Who may log in and do what**: connect Jenkins to your company's **single sign-on** (one login for all company tools) through the LDAP, SAML or OIDC plugins, and use **Matrix** or **Role-based** authorization so users see and run only what they need. Two common mistakes: letting anyone read without logging in, and "logged-in users can do anything".

**Credentials and scripts**: scope credentials to folders, keep the Groovy sandbox on, approve scripts sparingly, and limit who may configure jobs. Remember that anyone who can change a Jenkinsfile on a branch that gets built can run code with that job's credentials.

**Plugins** are the largest attack surface. Install few, update promptly, and watch the security advisories shown under **Manage Jenkins**.

**Growing**: one controller can serve many agents, but its CPU, memory and disk are shared by everyone. Use **ephemeral agents** from the Kubernetes or EC2 cloud plugins: a fresh pod or virtual machine per build, deleted afterwards, which gives isolation and capacity that grows with demand. Watch the build queue, executor use and the controller's memory pauses; split very large installations into several controllers, one per team, rather than growing one forever.
concepts.code:
# casc/jenkins.yaml (excerpt)
jenkins:
  numExecutors: 0                  # no builds on the controller
  authorizationStrategy:
    globalMatrix:
      entries:
        - group:
            name: authenticated
            permissions: ["Overall/Read", "Job/Read", "Job/Build"]
        - user:
            name: admin
            permissions: ["Overall/Administer"]
  clouds:
    - kubernetes:
        name: k8s
        namespace: ci
        containerCap: 50
        templates:
          - name: maven
            label: maven
            containers:            # a fresh pod per build, deleted afterwards
              - name: maven
                image: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21
                command: sleep
                args: infinity
takeaways: Zero executors on the controller; builds run on agents
Use single sign-on plus matrix or role-based authorization
Ephemeral Kubernetes or cloud agents give isolation and capacity on demand
pitfalls: Leaving executors on the built-in node, letting any job read the controller's secrets.

quiz.q: Why set the controller's number of executors to 0?
options: Builds there could read JENKINS_HOME, including secrets, and slow the controller down
quiz.explain: Builds on the controller can read its files, and compete with scheduling and the website for its resources.
